name: Design a Coordination Service
intent: Run a small replicated cluster that other systems trust for configuration, membership, locks and leader election, with strong guarantees on a tiny amount of data.
codeTitle: a replicated key tree with versions, watches, sessions and a lock
finalIntro: One worker taking a lock, doing its work, and handing over when it dies.
prompt: Design a coordination service like ZooKeeper or etcd. Hundreds of services use it to store small pieces of configuration, to discover each other, to elect a leader and to take locks. It must stay correct when machines fail, and it must tell clients when something they care about changes.
functional: Store small values in a hierarchical key space, such as /services/payments/instance-7
Read, write, delete and list the children of a key, with a version on each key
Conditional updates: write only if the version is still the one I read
Watches: tell me once when a key or its children change
Sessions with ephemeral keys that vanish when the client goes silent
Recipes for leader election and distributed locks built from these primitives
nonFunctional: Writes are linearizable: one global order that every client agrees on
Survive the loss of a minority of servers with no lost write and no wrong answer
A write commits in a few milliseconds inside one region, and a few thousand writes per second are enough
Reads are fast and can be served by any server, with a choice between fresh and possibly stale
Elect a new leader and resume within seconds of a failure
Keep the whole data set in memory, which means megabytes or a few gigabytes, never terabytes

firstAttempt.text: One server holding the key tree in a database. Clients read and write over HTTP, and poll for changes every few seconds. A lock is a row that a client inserts, and it removes the row when it is done.
limits: The one server is a single point of failure for every system that depends on it, which is the worst place for a single point of failure
Polling is slow and wasteful: changes are noticed late, and hundreds of clients repeat the same read
A client that crashes holding the lock never removes its row, so the lock stays taken forever
Two clients can both believe they hold the lock after a pause or a partition, with nothing to stop the older one
Simply copying to a second server by hand risks two servers both accepting writes and disagreeing

steps.title: Replicate the state over a few servers with one leader
steps.problem: A single server is a single point of failure for everything that depends on it, and two servers that both accept writes will disagree.
steps.fix: Run an odd number of servers, three to start. One is the leader, and every write goes through it. The leader appends the write to a log, sends it to the followers, and counts it as committed once a majority, including itself, has stored it. Only then does it apply the write and answer the client. All servers apply the same log in the same order, so they hold the same data. If the leader dies, the followers elect a new one, and only a server with all the committed entries can win.
steps.tradeoff: Any minority of servers can fail without losing a committed write or stopping service, and there is one order of writes for everybody. Each write waits for a round trip to a majority, so writes are slower than on a single machine, and writing is limited by the one leader.

steps.title: Give every key a version, and a tree to live in
steps.problem: Clients that read, decide and write will overwrite each other, and they need to organise thousands of related keys, such as every instance of every service.
steps.fix: Keys form a tree of paths such as /services/payments/instance-7, and a key can have both a small value and children. Every key carries a version that goes up with each change, and the write can say 'only if the version is still 4'. If someone else got in first, the write is refused and the client reads again and retries. Listing the children of a key is how clients discover each other. A key's creation and last change also record the position in the log, a number that only ever grows.
steps.tradeoff: Compare-and-set gives safe read-modify-write without any lock, and the tree makes discovery natural. Values are limited to about a megabyte or less, and a key with a hundred thousand children makes every listing heavy.

steps.title: Serve reads from followers, and say how fresh they are
steps.problem: If every read goes to the leader, the leader does all the work, and most traffic is reads.
steps.fix: Any server can answer a read from its own copy, so read capacity grows with the number of servers. A follower may be a little behind the leader, so a plain read can return an older value. A client sees its own writes and never goes backwards, because the follower tells it the log position it has reached and the client library refuses a server that is further behind than what it has already seen. A client that needs the latest value asks for a synchronised read, in which the follower first catches up with the leader, or asks the leader.
steps.tradeoff: Most reads are cheap and scale out, and the occasional strict read gets a fresh answer at the price of an extra round trip. A careless reader of a plain read can act on stale data, so the code that needs the latest value must say so.

steps.title: Add sessions, ephemeral keys and watches
steps.problem: Clients crash and leave stale entries behind, and polling for changes is both slow and expensive.
steps.fix: A client opens a session and sends a small heartbeat now and then. The session is itself replicated, so all servers agree on when it ends. Keys created as ephemeral belong to the session and are deleted by the cluster when the session expires or closes, so a crashed instance disappears from the service list by itself. A client can set a watch on a key or on a key's children, and the cluster sends one notification when it changes, after which the client reads again and sets a new watch. Notifications arrive in the same order as the changes.
steps.tradeoff: Liveness and change notification become part of the data model, with no polling. A session timeout trades speed of detection against false alarms from a slow network or a long pause in the client. A watch only says that something changed, so the client must read to find out what.

steps.title: Build locks and leader election as recipes
steps.problem: Services want a lock, or want exactly one of them to be the leader, and a naive version breaks when the holder crashes or when many clients wake up at once.
steps.fix: To take a lock, a client creates an ephemeral, sequential key under the lock's path, and the cluster appends an increasing number to its name. The client with the lowest number holds the lock. Every other client watches only the key just before its own, so when the holder releases or dies, exactly one waiter wakes. Leader election is the same recipe, with the lowest number as leader. The creation position of the lock holder's key serves as a fencing token, which the protected resource uses to refuse anyone older.
steps.tradeoff: Locks are released automatically on failure, there is a fair queue, and there is no stampede of waiters. A client that is paused for longer than its session can still believe it holds a lock that was given away, so the resource it protects must check the token, because the lock service cannot stop a stalled process.

steps.title: Size the cluster, add observers, and keep the data small
steps.problem: More servers means more failures tolerated, but every write has to reach a majority, and a service that is too popular can drag the whole cluster down.
steps.fix: Use three servers to tolerate one failure and five to tolerate two. Seven is rarely worth it, because each write waits on four servers. Spread the servers over three failure zones, so losing a zone loses at most one. Add non-voting observers to carry read and watch load for far-away or numerous clients, since they receive the log but do not count in the majority. Keep the data set in memory, take regular snapshots plus a log on disk so a restarted server recovers quickly, and enforce limits on value size and request rate per client.
steps.tradeoff: The cluster stays fast, and reads scale without slowing writes. This is a database for kilobytes of coordination data, and not for bulk data: every server keeps a full copy in memory, and every write goes to one leader and a majority, so using it as a general store would ruin it for everyone.

failures.impact: Writes stop until a new leader is chosen, and clients with a pending write do not know whether it was committed.
failures.answer: The followers notice the missing heartbeats, hold an election, and the server with the most complete log wins, so every committed write survives. The service resumes within seconds. A client retries its write with a version check, or an identifier, so that a write that did commit is not applied twice.

failures.scenario: A network partition splits five servers into 3 and 2
failures.impact: Both sides can still talk to some clients, and a leader on the small side could accept writes that the other side then contradicts.
failures.answer: Only the side with a majority, three of five, can commit. The two-server side cannot reach a majority, so it refuses writes and, for strict reads, cannot answer. Clients connected to it fail over to a server on the majority side. When the partition heals, the minority servers catch up from the log. Availability is given up on the small side so that nobody sees two truths.

failures.scenario: A lock holder stalls in a long garbage-collection pause
failures.impact: Its session expires, the lock goes to the next client, and then the old holder wakes up still believing it holds the lock.
failures.answer: The lock service cannot interrupt a paused process, so protection is placed at the resource. Each lock grant carries a fencing token that grows, and the storage or the downstream service remembers the highest token it has seen and refuses an older one. The old holder's write is rejected even though it is sure it holds the lock.

failures.scenario: Ten thousand clients all watch one key
failures.impact: When it changes, the cluster sends ten thousand notifications and then ten thousand clients read it again at once.
failures.answer: Observers take over the watch fan-out, so the voting servers do not carry it. Clients add a random delay before re-reading, and for hot keys a version number in the notification lets them skip the read when they are already up to date. Where possible, clients watch a parent key once instead of every child.

failures.scenario: The log and snapshots grow, and a restarted server takes minutes to recover
failures.impact: Replaying a long log delays the return of a failed server, and a slow disk slows every commit.
failures.answer: The server takes periodic snapshots of the in-memory tree and deletes the older part of the log. A restarted server loads the latest snapshot, replays the short tail, and fetches anything newer from the leader. The log goes on a dedicated fast disk, because every commit waits for it to be flushed.

alternatives.title: Where the consensus lives

options.name: A dedicated coordination cluster
options.pro: One well-understood place, shared by many systems, and tuned for small, critical data
options.con: Another cluster to run, monitor and keep healthy

options.name: A library inside each service
options.con: Each service reimplements a hard protocol, and many services run an election for themselves

options.name: A relational database with row locks
options.con: No watches or ephemeral keys, and failover is up to you

alternatives.pick: A dedicated cluster, and ideally a managed or well-proven one, because consensus code is very hard to get right.

alternatives.title: How strict reads should be

options.name: All reads linearizable, through the leader
options.con: The leader serves all traffic, so read capacity does not grow

options.name: Reads from any follower by default
options.pro: Scales with servers and stays up when the leader is busy
options.con: May return an older value, so some code must ask for more

options.name: Follower reads that are checked against the leader
options.pro: Fresh, and the leader only confirms its position
options.con: An extra round trip and extra leader work

alternatives.pick: Follower reads by default with a monotonic position per client, and a strict read where the decision depends on the latest value.

alternatives.title: How many voting servers

options.name: Three
options.pro: Cheapest and fastest, since a write waits for two
options.con: Tolerates one failure, and a failure during maintenance leaves no spare

options.name: Five
options.pro: Tolerates two failures, so you can take one down for maintenance and still survive another
options.con: A write waits for three and costs more machines

options.name: Seven
options.con: Slower writes and more traffic for a small gain, and rarely needed in one region

alternatives.pick: Five across three zones for production, and three for smaller or less critical setups.

alternatives.title: How a client learns about changes

options.name: Poll the key
options.pro: Simple, and the client controls the rate
options.con: Slow to notice, and a lot of repeated load

options.name: One-shot watches
options.pro: Immediate and cheap, and the client re-arms only after it has looked
options.con: A change between the notification and the re-arm must be caught by reading again

options.name: A persistent stream of changes from a revision
options.pro: Nothing is missed, since the client resumes from the last revision it saw
options.con: The server must keep history, and slow consumers need handling

alternatives.pick: Watches for small things. For a client that must never miss a change, a stream from a revision, as etcd offers.

roles.label: Clients
roles.description: Services that read configuration, register themselves and take locks.

roles.label: Entry points
roles.description: The client library and the observers that carry read and watch load.

roles.label: Notifications
roles.description: The watch manager that sends one-shot change events.

roles.label: Leader and logic
roles.description: The leader, the session tracker and the lock and election recipes.

roles.label: State
roles.description: The replicated log, the versioned key tree and the followers' copies.

quiz.question: A team takes a lock by inserting a row into a table, and deletes the row when done. A worker crashes while holding the lock, and every other worker now waits. What design removes this problem?
options: A cron job deletes any lock row older than 10 minutes, which lets a waiting worker take over after a crash
Workers poll the lock row every second to notice when the holder stops
An ephemeral key tied to the holder's session, removed when its heartbeats stop
A second database server copies the table, so a worker can reach the lock after a failure
quiz.explanation: The cluster itself ends the session and deletes the key, so a crash frees the lock without cleanup code. A 10-minute sweep waits too long and also steals locks from slow but healthy holders. Polling and replicas do not tell anyone the holder is dead.

quiz.question: A team runs three coordination servers and patches one at a time. During a patch, a second server crashes and writes stop. The team wants to survive a patch plus one real failure. Which cluster size fits?
options: Five voting servers across three zones, since a majority of three remains with two servers down
Four voting servers, since the extra machine gives one more copy of the data to fall back on
Three voting servers plus three observers, since the observers hold the data and can take over when a voter fails
Seven voting servers, since tolerating three failures covers any combination of patch and crash
quiz.explanation: With three servers a majority is two, so two down means no quorum. With five, a majority is three, so one patch plus one crash is fine. Four servers need three for a majority and tolerate only one failure. Observers do not vote. Seven works but makes each write wait for four servers for little gain.

quiz.question: A client holds a lock, then pauses in a 40-second garbage collection. Its session timeout is 10 seconds, so the lock moves to another client. The first client wakes and writes to shared storage. How is the data protected?
options: The lock service closes the paused client's connection so its write cannot arrive
Each lock grant carries a growing token, and storage refuses a write with an older token
The session timeout is raised to 5 minutes, so no ordinary pause is long enough for the lock to move to another client
The client checks that it still holds the lock just before each write, and writes only if the check passes
quiz.explanation: A stalled process cannot be stopped from outside, so the protected resource must check the token. A check just before the write can still be followed by a pause, so it races. A longer timeout only moves the limit and slows failure detection.
